holidays.name: National Tie Dye Day
holidays.description: Break out the rubber bands and squeeze bottles. This is a day for swirling, twisting, and soaking plain white cotton into a rainbow of color. Every shirt, sock, and pillowcase is fair game, and no two results ever match.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial observance, and its creator is unclear. It celebrates the colorful craft that became a symbol of 1960s counterculture.
holidays.funFact: Tie-dye is a form of resist dyeing. Tied or folded sections of cloth block the dye, which is why the patterns turn out so unpredictable. Similar techniques go back centuries in places like Japan (shibori), India (bandhani), and West Africa.

holidays.name: National Honesty Day
holidays.description: Today is for telling the truth, even when a fib would be easier. That means admitting you didn't read the group chat, and also admitting you don't love your friend's casserole. Tact is welcome. Fibbing is not.
holidays.origin: Author M. Hirsh Goldberg created it in the 1990s. He had written The Book of Lies and wanted a day to encourage truthfulness. Some say he chose April 30 as a counterweight to April Fools' Day.
holidays.funFact: Goldberg's book on lies helped inspire the day. Its purpose is to promote honesty in everyday life and public life alike.

holidays.name: National Oatmeal Cookie Day
holidays.description: Celebrate the chewy, cinnamon-kissed cookie that lets you call dessert a breakfast food. Raisins, chocolate chips, walnuts, and cranberries are all welcome. The only real debate is how soft to bake them.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial food observance of unclear origin. It gives oatmeal cookie fans a day to bake and share.
holidays.funFact: Oatmeal cookies are often tied to the Scottish tradition of oat-based baking. Oats have been a staple there for centuries, and the cookie grew from that tradition.
